3 WEEKS 1 AND 2:CRUDE OIL AND PETROCHEMICALS OBJECTIVES : ➢ Explain what crude oil and petrochemicals are. ➢ Describe the process of refining crude oil. ➢ State the uses of crude oil and petrochemicals. ➢ State the importance of crude oil to Nigeria Crude oil or petroleum is a dark, viscous liquid found in huge underground deposits in many parts of the world. It is formed in the rocks of the earth’s crust from the remains of marine animals and plants. It is a complex mixture of gases, liquids and solid hydrocarbons together with some impurities of sulphur, nitrogen and oxygen – sulphur being the most troublesome. Nigerian crude oil is relatively sulphur free and this makes it very marketable. CRUDE OIL REFINING AND TREATMENT OF FRACTIONS The separation of crude oil into various useful parts is called refining, and this is done in a refinery through a process called fractional distillation. The separation is carried out in tall towers called fractionating towers/columns.

4 The crude oil is heated in an electric furnace to a high temperature before being conducted in pipes to the fractionating column. In the fractionating column, the vapour of the different fractions/components of the crude oil rise at different speed and to different heights since they have different weights. The fraction with lower boiling points gets to the top while those with lower boiling points are obtained at the lower parts. An antiknock agent is a gasoline additive used to reduce engine knocking and increase the fuel's octane rating. Lead (II) tetra ethyl (Tetra-ethyl lead) is in common use. Octane Number: Octane number is a value used to indicate the resistance of a motor fuel to knock. Octane numbers are based on a scale from 0 to 100. A long, straight-chain alkane, which burns unevenly and produces a great deal of knocking has octane number of 0. Highly branched alkanes are more resistant to knocking have octane number of 100.

6 Further treatment of petroleum products 1. Cracking: Cracking is the breaking down of large hydrocarbon molecules (long-chained) into smaller hydrocarbons (short-chained) and more useful bits of fragments for use in gasoline. This is achieved by using high pressures and temperatures without a catalyst, or lower temperatures and pressures in the presence of a catalyst. Due to the high demand for petrol and other useful volatile crude oil fractions, the less volatile fractions such as diesel oil is converted to petrol by cracking. (a) Thermal cracking: In thermal cracking, high temperatures (about 450°C to 750°C) and pressures (up to about 70 atmospheres) are used to break the large hydrocarbons into smaller ones. Thermal cracking gives mixtures of products containing high proportions of hydrocarbons with double bonds - alkenes. (b) Catalytic cracking: Involvesheating long chain hydrocarbons under pressure and in the presence of catalyst. The alkane is brought into contact with the catalyst at a temperature of about 500°C and moderately low pressures. Modern cracking uses zeolites as the catalyst. These are complex aluminosilicates, containing aluminium, silicon and oxygen atoms. You may have come across a zeolite if you know about ion exchange resins used in water softeners. NOTE: Catalytic cracking produces petrol mixture rich in branch chain hydrocarbon with an attendant increase in octane number more than thermal cracking. Cracking is a breaking down process while reforming is an isomerization process. 2. Reforming: This is the process of rearranging the structure of petroleum products (e.g. petrol) to improve its anti-knock properties. It is a chemical process used to convert petroleum refinery naphtha, typically having low octane ratings, into high-octane liquid products called reformates which are components of high-octane gasoline (also known as high-octane petrol). Reforming is used to improve the quality of petrol by converting straight- chain hydrocarbons to branch-chain and cyclic hydrocarbons which yield high performance fuels. Hydrogen is produced as a by-product of the reactions. Types of reforming (a) Thermal reforming.

7 (b) Catalytic reforming: While thermal reforming could produce reformate with octane numbers of 65-80 depending on the yield, catalytic reforming produces reformate with octane numbers on the order of 90-95. Reforming and gasoline additives such as tetraethyl lead increase the octane number of the straight-run gasoline obtained from the fractional distillation of crude oil, but neither process increases the yield of gasoline from a barrel of oil. PETROCHEMICALS Petrochemicals are substances that are manufactured from the by-products of petroleum. These include plastics, nylon, Dacron, synthetic rubber, insecticides, inorganic fertilizers, benzene, toluene, synthesis gas and detergents Some chemical compounds made from petroleum are also obtained from other fossil fuels, such as coal or natural gas, or renewable sources such as corn or sugar cane. Major End Use Products: Some typical petrochemical intermediates are: - Vinyl acetate for paint, paper and textile coatings vinyl chloride for polyvinyl chloride (PVC) for water pipes electrical installations. - Resin manufacture for zeolites etc. - Ethylene glycol for polyester - textile fibers - Styrene which is important in rubber and plastic manufacturing. - Benzene for nylon acid.

9 WEEK 3: CHEMICAL SYMBOLS AND FORMULAE OBJECTIVES i. Define chemical symbol. ii. Write the symbols of the first twenty elements. A chemical symbol is the abbreviation for the name of an element. It is a letter or letters representing the name of an element. There are four ways of writing the symbols of elements. 1. By using the first letter of the name of the element. The symbol is written in capital letter. Examples are: Name of element Symbol Hydrogen H Boron B Oxygen O Nitrogen N Fluorine F Phosphorus P Sulphur S 2. By using the first two letters of the name of the element. The first letter of the symbol is written as a capital letter, while the second letter is written as a small letter. Examples are: Name of element Symbol Helium He Lithium Li Beryllium Be Neon Ne Aluminium Al Silicon Si Argon Ar Calcium Ca 3. By using the first letter and any other letter in the name of the element. The first letter of the symbol is written as a capital letter, while the second letter is written as a small letter. Examples are:

English name of element Latin name Symbol Sodium Natrium Na Iron Ferrum Fe Copper Cuprum Cu Potassium Kalium K Silver Argentum Ag Gold Aurum Au Lead Plumbum Pb Mercury Hydrargyrum Hg CHEMICAL FORMULAE This is a shorthand representation which shows the kind and number of atoms in one molecule of a compound. It is the representation of an element, a molecule or a compound by using symbols of atoms. It is represented by letters and numerals. The letters represent the symbol of the element, while the numerals represent the number of atoms in the molecule or compound. IUPAC Nomenclature (name) of inorganic compounds IUPAC means international union of pure and applied chemistry. It is the body of chemists that agrees on the names of chemical substances in order to have uniform name for a particular substance all over the world. Naming of binary compounds A binary compound is a compound that is made up of two substances (elements or radicals). Note: That OH-, NH4+ and CN- radicals are considered as single element when present in a compound therefore Ca(OH)2, NaCN, NH4Cl etc. are binary compounds. Rules in Naming Binary Compounds

11 Rule 1: The first element, which may be a metal or a non-metal, is named first. Where the first element is NH4+, it is named first as ammonium. Rule 2: If the first element has a variable oxidation numbers as in Cu = +1 and +2, Fe = +2 and +3, Hg = +1 and +2, Au = +1 and +3, Mn = +2, +4 and +7, Cr = +3 and +6, N = +1 to + 5, S = +2, +4 and +6, the oxidation number of the element is written in roman figure and is indicated in bracket after the name of the first element e.g. Iron (ii), Sulphur (vi), Nitrogen (iii), Copper (I), Tin (iv). Rule 3: The second element which is usually a non-metal is named by replacing the last 2, 3 or 4 letters of their name by letter –ide. E.g. * Carbon as Carbide * Chlorine as Chloride * Sulphur as Sulphide * Oxygen as Oxide * Hydrogen as Hydride * Fluorine as Fluoride * Phosphorus as Phosphide * Bromine as Bromide Where the second element is OH- or CN- radical, it is named as hydroxide or cyanide. The empirical formula is the simplest formula for a compound. The empirical formula is the ratio of elements present in the compound. A molecular formula is the same as or a multiple of the empirical formula, and is based on the actual number of atoms of each type in the compound.

15 The molecular formula is the number and type of atoms that are present in a single molecule of a substance. For example, if the empirical formula of a compound is C3H8, its molecular formula may be C3H8 , C6H16 , etc.

Law of Conservation of Matter: It states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed during chemical reactions.

19 Experiment to verify the law of conservation of matter. Procedure: Using the precipitation reaction between sodium chloride (NaCl) solution and silver trioxonitrate (v) solution. Solution of sodium chloride is put inside a conical flask and a solution of silver trioxonitrate (v) is put inside a test tube which is suspended inside the conical flak by means of two strings that are attached to the test tube. The conical flask is corked using a rubber cork and it is weighed. After the weighing, pull the bottom string of the test tube so that the AgNO3 solution is poured into the flask for chemical reaction to take place between the NaCl(aq) and the AgNO3(aq) Observation: A white precipitate of silver chloride is formed as a result of chemical reaction between the NaCl(aq) and the AgNO3(aq). The flask is then weighed again. AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq) Reactants Products Results: It is found that the mass of the reactants before the chemical reaction is the same as the mass of the silver chloride product at the end of the chemical reaction and thus the law of conservation of matter is verified. 2. Law of Constant Composition or Definite Proportion: It states that all pure samples of the same chemical compound contain the same elements combined in the same proportion by mass.

23 WEEK 6: CHEMICAL EQUATIONS OBJECTIVES: i. Write the equation for the reaction between HCl and CaCO3 to form water, CO2 and CaCl2. ii. Balance simple chemical equations. A chemical reaction takes place when different elements combine with each other to form a new substance. A chemical equation therefore is a condensed or shorthand statement about a chemical reaction. It represents the changes in bonding and energy that takes place during a chemical reaction. A chemical equation has two parts: i. The right-hand side i.e., the product side ii. The left-hand side i.e., the reactant side. H2(g) + O2(g) H2O(l) reactants product The plus sign means “reacting with” while the arrow sign means “produce” or “yield” or “give”. A chemical equation describes what happens in a chemical reaction. The equation identifies the reactants (starting materials) and products (resulting substance), the formulas of the participants, the phases of the participants (solid, liquid, gas), and the amount of each substance. BALANCING CHEMICAL EQUATIONS Balancing a chemical equation refers to establishing the mathematical relationship between the quantity of reactants and products. The quantities are expressed as grams or moles. A chemical equation is a condensed statement of a chemical reaction. It represents the changes in bonding and energy that takes place in a reaction. According to the law of conservation of matter/mass, atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, they are only changed from one form to another. So, the total number of an atom present in the reactant side must be equal to the total number of the same atom present on the product side. We use coefficients to indicate the smallest number of molecules of a substance that can take part in a chemical reaction. COEFFICIENTS are numbers written in front of formulae to balance the equation. A balanced equation accounts for all the atoms taking part in a chemical reaction both in number and in kind. It takes practice to be able to write balanced equations.

26 WEEK 8 CHEMICAL REACTIONS OBJECTIVES: By the end of the lesson, students should be able to; i. Differentiate between exothermic and endothermic reactions. ii. Give THREE examples EACH of exothermic and endothermic reactions. A chemical reaction is a process that is usually characterized by a chemical change in which the starting materials (reactants) are different from the products. Chemical reactions tend to involve the motion of electrons, leading to the formation and breaking of chemical bonds. There are several different types of chemical reactions and more than one way of classifying them. Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions: During a chemical reaction, heat can be evolved or absorbed depending on the relative heat content of the reactants and the products. When the total heat content of the products is less than that of the reactants, the excess energy will be given off as heat to the surrounding as the reaction occurs. This type of reaction is said to be exothermic. When the total heat content of the product is more than that of the reactants, heat energy must be absorbed from the surroundings for the reaction to proceed. Such a reaction is said to be endothermic. An exothermic reaction is one during which heat is liberated to the surroundings. An endothermic reaction is one during which heat is absorbed from the surroundings. Some examples of exothermic reactions are as follows: 1. Reaction between calcium oxide and water CaO(s) + H2O Ca(OH)2(s) 2. Reaction between an acid and a base HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) Some examples of endothermic reactions are as follows: 1. Thermal decomposition of calcium trioxocarbonate (IV) CaCO3(s)CaO(s) + CO2(g) 2. Thermal dissociation of ammonium chloride NH4Cl(s) NH3(g) + HCl(g)Heat

28 Heat WEEKS9 AND 10: TYPES OF REACTIONS OBJECTIVES i. List SIX types of chemical reactions ii. Define combination reaction. iii. Differentiate between the following pairs: (a) Thermal decomposition reaction and thermal dissociation. (b) Homogeneous catalysis and heterogeneous catalysis Chemical reactions are changes in which new chemical substances are formed. Chemical reactions can be grouped as: ➢ Combination ➢ Decomposition ➢ Displacement ➢ Double decomposition ➢ Catalytic reaction ➢ Reversible reactions ➢ Thermal dissociation ➢ Oxidation and reduction 1. Combination reaction: This is a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form a single compound. Combinations can occur in any one of the following ways: Element + element compound e.g Fe(s) + S(s)FeS(s) Compound + compound bigger compound e.g. PbO2(s) + SO2(g) PbSO4(s) Many organic compounds also undergo combination reactions. The polymerization of ethyne, for example, is a special type of combination reaction. 2. Decomposition reaction: This is a reaction in which a single compound split up into two or more simpler substances. When heat is needed to bring about decomposition, the reaction is called thermal decomposition. 2Pb(NO3)2(s) 2PbO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g) 3. Displacement reaction: This is a reaction in which an element (or a radical) replaces another element (or a radical) in a compound. The ability of an element to displace another is determined by their relative positions in the electrochemical series. Thus more electropositive metals will displace less electropositive metals from their aqueous solutions. E.g.

29 NO(g) Fe(s) Ni(S) Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s) Also, more electronegative non-metal will displace less electronegative non-metals from their aqueous solutions. E.g. Cl2(g) + 2KBr(aq) 2KCl(aq) + Br2(l) 4. Double decomposition: This is a reaction in which the reactants decompose to form new substances by an exchange of radicals. The two reactants are soluble while one of the products is soluble while the other is insoluble, volatile or gaseous. E.g. AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq) 5. Catalytic reaction: This is a chemical reaction during which a catalyst is used. The acceleration or retardation of reactions by catalysts is known as catalysis. A catalyst is a substance which alters the rate of a chemical reaction, but which itself remains chemically and quantitatively unchanged at the end of the reaction. There are two types of catalysed reactions and these are: i. Homogeneous catalysis: This is a catalysed reaction in which the catalyst, reactants and products are all in the same phase. E.g. 2SO2(g) + O2(g) 2SO3(g) ii. Heterogeneous catalysis: This is a catalysed reaction in which the catalyst, reactants and products are in the different phase. E.g. Vegetable oil(l) + H2(g) margarine(s) N2(g) + 3H2(g) 2NH3(g) NOTE: Since catalysts do not affect the overall reaction, they are written above the arrow in an equation. Characteristics of a catalyst i. A catalyst alters the rate of a chemical reaction. ii. It remains unchanged in chemical nature and in mass at the end of a reaction. Its physical features like colour and texture may change. iii. A catalyst is specific in action i.e. a given catalyst will act on only one particular reaction. Many inorganic catalysts can catalyse more than one reaction. iv. A catalyst cannot start a reaction. It only affects a reaction which is already in progress. v. A catalyst does not affect the type of product formed in a reaction. vi. A catalyst has no effect on the equilibrium of a reversible reaction. vii. A catalyst will affect the rate of a reaction even though it is present in very small amounts. An increase in the amount of catalyst up to a certain limit would usually increase the reaction rate.

30 MnO2 Hindered by H3PO4 Fe(s) In the cold Heat Heat Cool viii. The effect of a solid catalyst is improved by increasing its surface area. Types of catalysts a. Inorganic catalysts: These are catalysts that are mineral elements or compounds. They can be grouped into: i. Positive catalysts: These are catalysts which increases the rate of chemical reactions. E.g. 2KClO3(s) 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g) ii. Negative catalysts: These are catalysts which decreases the rate of chemical reactions. E.g. 2H2O2(l) 2H2O(l) + O2(g) b. Organic catalysts: These are known as enzymes. Enzymes are organic catalysts which control the rate of biochemical reactions in living organisms. They are produced by living cells. They help to digest food, cause blood to clot, make palm wine and fruit juices ferment and are also used in the industrial manufacture of alcohol from sugars and starches. Promoters and inhibitors: These are not catalysts but they influence the rate of a reaction by affecting the efficiency of the catalysts. Promoters are substances which improve the efficiency of a catalyst. N2(g) + 3H2(g) 2NH3(g) The iron catalyst used in Haber process is activated by the addition of trace amounts of aluminium oxide or molybdenum. Inhibitors are substances which reduces the efficiency of a catalyst. They are also known as catalyst poisons. Hydrogen sulphide, arsenic (III) oxide, hydrogen cyanide and mercury salts are catalyst poisons which harm us by inhibiting important enzymes in the body. 6. Reversible reactions: A reversible reaction is a chemical reaction where the reactants form products that in turn react together/split to give the reactants back. Reversible reactions will reach an equilibrium point where the concentrations of the reactants and products will no longer change. A reversible reaction is denoted by a double arrow pointing both directions in a chemical equation. The conditions for the reverse reaction may or may not be the same as the conditions for the forward reaction. Examples of reversible reactions are: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g) CaCO3(s) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) Ca(HCO3)2(aq) 7. Thermal dissociation: This is a chemical reaction in which a reactant molecule separates into two or more simpler molecules or atoms on the application of heat.
